perplexed: Not sure what to think or do; mixed up.
roundabout: A short coat that fits close to the body. Boys wore it in the old days.
lick: To beat someone in a fight, or to hit as a way to teach a child. A 'lick' is a hit.
obleeged: A spoken spelling of 'obliged'. It means must do something.
whitewash: White paint made with water and a white powder from stone. People put it on fences and walls.
taw: The big round glass ball that a player shoots at the other balls in the game.
morosely: In a sad way, with a bad feeling.
tallow: Hard fat from animals. People used it to make light and to keep things dry.
audacious: Showing no fear of what other people think; very brave and rude.
benediction: Words said at the end of a church meeting, asking God to bless the people.
scarify: To make small cuts or lines on something. Here, the new knife makes lines on the cupboard.
counterfeited: Made to look real, to trick people. Here it means a false copy of a real Barlow knife.
disconcerted: Upset and mixed up because something went wrong.
cravat: A wide cloth that a man wears around his neck.
sheepish: Shy and a little ashamed, like a person who knows he did wrong.
tittering: Quiet laughing that you try to keep inside.
supplication: A serious request made in a low voice, especially to God.
prosy: Dull because it is too long and says nothing new.
brimstone: A yellow stone that gives a bad smell when it burns. 'Fire and brimstone' is about the fires of hell.
fillip: A quick push made with a finger that is held back by the thumb and then let go.
mortified: In this story, about a part of the body that has died and is going bad. Tom says this about his toe.
gaudy: With too many bright colors. Here, Tom likes Huck's wild life outside the rules.
spunk: In 'spunk-water', rain water in an old tree that is going bad. The boys think it can take warts away.
wart: A small, hard bit that grows on the skin.
ferule: A flat stick. A teacher used it to hit the hand of a pupil.
gable: The top part of the end wall of a house, up under the roof.
portentous: Looking very important and a little scary.
tick: A very small animal that bites. The boys play with one.
grisly: Very bad to look at; it makes you afraid.
doublet: A short, tight coat that men wore long ago.
cutlass: A short, heavy, curved sword used on ships long ago.
shingle: A thin flat piece of wood.
caitiff: An old word for a bad man who is weak and has no courage.
lath: A thin, narrow piece of wood. The boys use laths as swords to play with.
doodlebug: A small animal that lives in a hole in the ground. The boys think it can answer questions.
ensconced: Settled in a safe place where nobody can see.
caterwauling: The loud, ugly crying that cats make at night.
deathwatch: A small animal that makes a clicking sound in wood. People thought it meant that someone would die.
pallid: Very white in the face, like a sick person.
tannery: A place where the skin of animals is made into leather.
verdigrease: The green poison that forms on brass or copper. Tom says a brass pin may have it on it.
escapade: An exciting thing to do that is against the rules.
phase: A spoken spelling of 'faze': to trouble or upset someone.
electrified: Made to feel a sudden, strong shock.
ostentatiously: In a way that is made to be seen by everyone.
palsy: An illness that makes the body shake.
coroner: An officer who finds out how a person died. In the boys' game, the leader of a pretend meeting for a dead cat.
infatuated: Filled with a strong love for something that is not good or not wise.
inveterate: Always doing something, because it is a strong habit.
havoc: Great damage and a big mess.
crestfallen: Sad and ashamed because things did not go as you wanted.
smouldering: Burning slowly with smoke but no fire to see.
freebooters: Men who take things from others by force; pirates.
quicksilver: A shiny silver metal that is a liquid. Today it is called mercury.
mutiny: When the people on a ship refuse to do what the leader says and act against him.
quartering: Going across a river at a slant, not straight across.
ejaculations: Short, sudden cries or words said out loud.
weltering: Lying in something and rolling in it. Here, Tom is crying so much that he is lost in his tears.
snifter: A small amount of strong drink, or of smoke. Joe says one little bit would be too much for Johnny Miller.
charily: Carefully, in a way that shows you are not sure.
hendering: A country spelling of 'hindering': keeping someone from doing something.
spume: White foam on water. 'Spumeflakes' are bits of this foam.
scalped: Cut the skin and hair from the head of an enemy, as some fighters did long ago.
soliloquized: Spoke out loud to herself when alone.
pregnant: Full of meaning. Here, 'pregnant with prophecy' means full of signs of what would happen.
funereal: Sad and slow, as at a funeral.
transfixed: Not able to move, because of shock.
rascalities: Bad acts that are naughty or not honest.
cowhide: A strong whip made from the skin of a cow. It was used to beat people.
abashed: Ashamed and not knowing what to do.
slink: To go away quietly, because you feel ashamed.
artlessly: In a simple, honest way, with no plan to trick anyone.
humiliated: Feeling ashamed and made to look silly.
mercury: In 'a sudden falling of his mercury', a silver liquid in a glass tube that shows how warm it is. Here, Tom's good feeling goes down.
softy: A person who is too gentle and easy to trick.
dominie: A word for a schoolmaster, used in Scotland.
gawky: Tall and awkward, not knowing how to move.
declamatory: In the style of a loud, formal speech.
voluptuous: Full of nice feelings for the body and the senses.
gilded: Covered with a thin layer of gold paint.
scuttle: A small opening with a cover, in a roof or floor.
minstrel: In this story, a show with songs and jokes by actors.
mesmerizer: A person who puts others into a sleep-like state to show tricks.
forbearance: Patience; not showing anger and not hitting back.
toils: A trap made of nets or ropes. Here, the law is closing around Potter like a trap.
diffident: Not sure of yourself, and so quiet.
hieroglyphics: Pictures and signs used as writing. The boys say it as 'hy'roglyphics'.
sepulchral: Sounding deep and sad, like a voice from a grave.
ha'nted: A spoken spelling of 'haunted': visited by ghosts.
